data.name: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis
data.description: LAM - a rare progressive cystic lung disease in women driven by inappropriate mTOR activation; sirolimus stabilizes lung function for as long as it is taken (MILES trial), with decline resuming after the drug is stopped.
data.description_beginner: LAM - a rare lung disease, almost always in women, in which mTOR gets stuck in the 'on' position and slowly destroys healthy lung tissue with cysts. The mTOR-blocking drug sirolimus is an approved treatment that keeps lung function from declining further for as long as it is taken: in the MILES trial, decline started again after the drug was stopped.

reading_levels.student: TSC-related proliferative lung disease treated with sirolimus.
reading_levels.research: MILES tested sirolimus and stabilised FEV1; EXIST-2 tested everolimus against renal angiomyolipoma, not the lung disease – a distinction routinely blurred.

studies.title: Everolimus for angiomyolipoma associated with tuberous sclerosis complex or sporadic lymphangioleiomyomatosis (EXIST-2): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
studies.authors: Bissler JJ; Kingswood JC; Radzikowska E; Zonnenberg BA; Frost M; Belousova E; Sauter M; Nonomura N; Brakemeier S; de Vries PJ; Whittemore VH; Chen D; Sahmoud T; Shah G; Lincy J; Lebwohl D; Budde K

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: The companion phase 3 RCT (n=118) to EXIST-1, targeting kidney tumors (angiomyolipomas) in tuberous sclerosis and LAM. Everolimus shrank them by >=50% in 42% of patients versus 0% on placebo. Together EXIST-1 and -2 sealed everolimus as a disease-modifying therapy across multiple TSC tumor types.

studies.title: Efficacy and safety of sirolimus in lymphangioleiomyomatosis (MILES)
studies.authors: McCormack FX; Inoue Y; Moss J; Singer LG; Strange C; Nakata K; Barker AF; Chapman JT; Brantly ML; Stocks JM; Brown KK; Lynch JP; Goldberg HJ; Young LR; Kinder BW; Downey GP; Sullivan EJ; Colby TV; McKay RT; Cohen MM; Korbee L; Taveira-DaSilva AM; Lee HS; Krischer JP; Trapnell BC

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: MILES was a 12-month placebo-controlled trial of sirolimus in 89 women with lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a rare lung disease driven by overactive mTOR. On placebo, lung function (FEV1) fell by about 12 ml a month. On sirolimus it held steady (+1 ml a month), a 153 ml difference over the year. In the next year nobody took the drug, and the sirolimus group's decline resumed in parallel with placebo, so the benefit lasted only while the drug was taken. Walking distance and gas-transfer capacity did not improve. Boundary: patients had fairly advanced disease (average FEV1 about 48% of predicted), many dropped out of the observation year, and mouth ulcers and rashes may have revealed who was on the drug. Sirolimus was held at a blood level of 5 to 15 ng/ml, so this was continuous dosing, not intermittent.

relations.mechanism: The MILES trial: sirolimus stabilised lung function (FEV1) in lymphangioleiomyomatosis while patients took it, and decline resumed after stopping. This - not the everolimus angiomyolipoma trial - is the evidence that mTOR inhibition treats LAM lung disease.
relations.mechanism_beginner: In a clinical trial, rapamycin stabilised lung function in a rare lung disease while patients kept taking it – the decline came back once they stopped.
relations.boundary: Benefit is suppressive: lung function declined again after withdrawal.
relations.note: Added 2026-07-29. EVE-LAM previously carried this claim on a trial whose endpoint was renal angiomyolipoma.
